Question: Let \(P(x) = (x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3).\) For how many polynomials \(Q(x)\) does there exist a polynomial \(R(x)\) of degree \(3\) such that \(P(Q(x)) = P(x) \cdot R(x)?\)
Solution:
The degree condition first restricts the possible form of \(Q\). Since \(R\) has degree 3, the polynomial \(P(x)R(x)\) is nonzero and has degree 6. Thus \(Q\) cannot be constant. If \(Q\) has degree \(d\ge1\), the leading term of \(P(Q(x))\) comes from \(Q(x)^3\), so its degree is \(3d\). Therefore \(3d=6\), and \(Q\) must be quadratic.

Next use the roots of \(P\). By the factor theorem, the three distinct factors \(x-1,x-2,x-3\) all divide \(P(Q(x))\) exactly when
\[
P(Q(1))=P(Q(2))=P(Q(3))=0.
\]
The only roots of \(P\) are \(1,2,3\). Consequently the divisibility condition is equivalent to
\[
Q(1),Q(2),Q(3)\in\{1,2,3\}.
\]
There are \(3^3=27\) possible ordered value triples. To count polynomials from these triples, we must check that each triple determines exactly one polynomial of degree at most 2.

Let the prescribed values be \(u,v,w\), and write
\[
Q(x)=\alpha(x-2)^2+\beta(x-2)+\gamma.
\]
Substituting \(x=1,2,3\) forces
\[
\gamma=v,\qquad
\beta=\frac{w-u}{2},\qquad
\alpha=\frac{u-2v+w}{2}.
\]
These coefficients both exist and are uniquely determined, so different value triples give different polynomials. The polynomial is quadratic precisely when \(\alpha\ne0\), or \(u+w\ne2v\).

There are exactly five triples with \(u+w=2v\). If \(v=1\), then \(u=w=1\); if \(v=3\), then \(u=w=3\). If \(v=2\), the pairs \((u,w)\) are \((1,3),(2,2),(3,1)\). These give the excluded triples
\[
(1,1,1),\ (2,2,2),\ (3,3,3),\
(1,2,3),\ (3,2,1).
\]
Every remaining triple gives a genuine quadratic for which \(P(x)\) divides \(P(Q(x))\). The quotient then has degree \(6-3=3\), so it supplies an allowed \(R\).

Thus the number of polynomials is \(27-5=\boxed{22}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
